newsitem.title: Cyprus: Turkish Cypriots warn missile row only on hold.
newsitem.headline: Turkish Cypriots warn missile row only on hold.

text.p: Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash warned on Monday that a tense row with Greek Cypriots over missile deployment could flare up again despite U.S. attempts to defuse the crisis.
"We will do all that is necessary in order to avert the arrival of the missiles," Denktash told reporters after meeting U.S. envoy Carey Cavanaugh in the north of the divided island.
The Russian-made S-300 system, which Turkey last week threatened to destroy, is not due to be installed in the Greek Cypriot south for more than a year.
"After 16 months, if they arrive, they create the crisis again," Denktash said. "Turkey has made it absolutely clear that it will not allow the missiles to come," he said.
U.S. State Department official Cavanaugh earlier said there was no crisis in Cyprus because its government had assured him it would not deploy the missiles for at least 16 months.
"I believe that should effectively defuse this as a crisis issue for Cyprus," he said after an hour-long meeting with Cypriot President Glafcos Clerides in the Greek Cypriot south of the island.
A senior Turkish official in Ankara dismissed the importance of the time factor.

"It doesn't make any difference to the Turkish side whether missiles are installed on the island today, tomorrow or 16 months later," the state-run Anatolian news agency quoted the unnamed official as saying. "Turkey's position is clear," he said.
Turkey invaded the northern third of Cyprus in 1974 in response to a Greek Cypriot coup attempt and has since kept 30,000 troops stationed there.
Turkish armed forces chief General Ismail Hakki Karadayi met with Denktash on Monday in a show of support for the breakaway Turkish Cypriot state, which is only recognised by Ankara.
Karadayi said the intended purchase of Russian-made missiles was the latest in a Greek Cypriot armament campaign aimed against Turkey.
"I see the Greek Cypriot decision to buy the S-300 missiles as the culmination of provocation and over-militarisation," he said.
"Let no one forget what the real purpose is," he told reporters at Ercan airport in the Turkish Cypriot sector.
Turkey says the missiles would have an offensive aim because they could hit planes inside Turkish airspace. Cyprus is 80 km (50 miles) from the Turkish mainland.
Karadayi said it was unacceptable to describe as defensive a weapons system that has a range of 150 to 160 km (93 to 100 miles).
The Greek Cypriot administration, recognised internationally as the island's only government, says it needs the S-300s to counter any Turkish air strike.
The Cypriot government on Monday allayed fears of imminent conflict with Turkey but vowed to proceed with the missile deployment.
"What is needed right now is the concentration on efforts for a political solution to the Cyprus problem," spokesman Yiannakis Cassoulides said after U.S. envoy Cavanaugh met President Clerides.
